summary: Defines a general framework for the metrics developed by the IETF's IP Performance Metrics effort. It lays out concepts and methods so that measurements of things like delay and packet loss are defined clearly and can be compared.

eli5.summary: A rulebook for measuring how fast and reliable the internet is, so everyone measures with the same ruler.

questions: what is wire time in network measurement
subtitle: The shared vocabulary and ground rules for defining Internet performance metrics so that measurements mean the same thing to everyone.

tldr.problem: Users and providers of Internet service need an accurate common understanding of performance and reliability, but loosely defined measurements are ambiguous and hard to repeat.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets criteria for metrics and defines terms for paths and clouds, analytical and empirical metrics, composition, clock and wire-time issues, singletons, samples and statistics, Poisson sampling, packet types and standard-formed packets.
tldr.outcome: Later RFCs define the individual metrics on top of this framework. The memo is Informational and has been updated by RFC 7312, RFC 8468 and RFC 9198.

today: RFC 2330 is an Informational memo and has been updated by RFC 7312, RFC 8468 and RFC 9198. It defines concepts and rules rather than specific metrics, which the RFC says would get separate RFCs.

sections.title: Goals and Criteria for Metrics
sections.content:
The memo is a general framework for the particular metrics to be developed by the IETF's IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) effort, which began in the Benchmarking Methodology Working Group. The overarching goal is that users and providers of Internet transport service share an accurate understanding of the performance and reliability of the clouds they use or provide.

To get there, the RFC lists criteria. Metrics must be concrete and well defined. A methodology must be repeatable: used many times under identical conditions, it gives consistent measurements. Metrics must show no bias for clouds built with identical technology, and an understood and fair bias for non-identical technology. They must be useful to users and providers, and must avoid inducing artificial performance goals.

Text inside curly-bracket Comment blocks is only commentary, not part of the framework and not a proposal of any specific metric.
sections.eli5: Everyone who measures the internet should use rules that are clear, can be repeated, and are fair to every kind of network.

sections.title: Paths, Clouds and Exchanges
sections.content:
The RFC defines a small vocabulary. A host is a computer that speaks Internet protocols, including routers. A link is a single link-level connection between hosts. A path is a sequence of hosts and links from h0 to hn, where the middle hosts are routers. A path is a unidirectional concept, and a pair of a link and the host after it is a hop.

A cloud is an undirected graph whose vertices are routers and whose edges are links. An exchange is a special link that connects a host to a cloud or one cloud to another. A path digest is a path summarized as hosts, exchanges and cloud subpaths. This lets a measurement on a whole path be discussed piece by piece.
sections.eli5: A path is the route a package takes, one way. A cloud is a whole neighborhood of connected routers that you drive through without caring about the streets inside.

sections.title: Metrics, Methodologies and Composition
sections.content:
A metric is a carefully specified quantity related to performance or reliability. Difficulty in practical measurement is sometimes allowed, but ambiguity in meaning is not. Units follow the metric system, the unit of information is the bit, metric prefixes on bits mean powers of 1000 rather than 1024, and times are given in UTC.

A metric can be analytically specified, using concepts from the shared engineering framework (the A-frame), such as the propagation time of a link. Or it can be empirically specified by describing a reference methodology, for example the best flow capacity along a path using a particular TCP. Several methodologies can exist for one metric, such as direct measurement with injected traffic or projection from lower-level measurements, and a good one is repeatable and shows continuity: small changes in conditions give small changes in results.

Metrics may exhibit spatial composition (a path metric relates to the same metric on subpaths) or temporal composition (a value at time T relates to values at earlier times). Any such claim must come with the specific conjecture and a justification of its practical use. Measurement errors must be minimized, understood, documented and quantified.
sections.eli5: A metric is a well-defined question like how long a package takes. You can answer it by doing the math on how the network works or by actually trying it. Either way the question has to be crystal clear.

sections.title: Clocks and Wire Time
sections.content:
Many metrics depend on time, so imperfect clocks matter. The RFC borrows NTP terminology (RFC 1305) and defines a clock's offset (reported time minus true UTC time), accuracy, skew (the frequency difference from true time), drift (change in skew) and resolution (the smallest unit by which the clock updates). For two clocks it uses relative versions and a joint resolution. Two clocks with zero relative offset are synchronized, which for many measurements matters more than accuracy to true time.

Using NTP to calibrate such measurements can be unsound, because NTP's accuracy depends on the delay of the same paths being measured. The RFC gives an example: with a skew of 0.01% (1 part in 10,000), after 10 minutes of observation the error in a one-way delay measurement is 60 ms, which can wipe out the accuracy of a transmission delay near 50 ms. It therefore favors clocks that take time directly from a source such as GPS.

The RFC also defines wire arrival time (the first time any bit of a packet appears at a host's observation point on a link) and wire exit time (the first time all the bits have appeared). Metrics should be defined in terms of wire times rather than host endpoint times where appropriate, so that host delays are separated from network delays.
sections.eli5: If two stopwatches disagree, your race times are wrong. Also, you should note when the package actually left the door, not when you decided to send it.

sections.title: Singletons, Samples and Poisson Sampling
sections.content:
The RFC separates three notions. A singleton metric is atomic, such as one measurement of delay. A sample is a number of singletons taken together, and a statistic is something computed from a sample, such as a mean.

For collecting samples, fixed-interval periodic sampling is simple but can miss periodic behavior, is easy to anticipate and manipulate, and the measurements can themselves synchronize a network. The preferred approach is Poisson sampling: the gaps between measurements are independent exponentially distributed random numbers, so the next sample time cannot be predicted and the sample is unbiased. Intervals can be generated with Ei = -log(Ui) / lambda from uniform random numbers Ui. Three methods approximate it, with method 1 the easiest but least accurate and method 3 (precompute a schedule of times) the hardest but potentially error-free.

Measurements should be checked for self-consistency, for example by flagging a negative round trip time as an error to investigate. Distributions are described with the empirical distribution function, and goodness-of-fit is judged with the Anderson-Darling test at 5% significance. The appendix gives C code for it and notes that a significance level of -1 is returned when n is less than 5.
sections.eli5: If you check on something at exactly the same time every day, you might always catch it in the same mood. Checking at random moments gives a truer picture.

sections.title: Packet Types, Addresses and Standard-Formed Packets
sections.content:
Metric definitions avoid stochastic terms. Instead of a packet loss probability they define a packet loss rate, such as 73 packets out of 100, so that hidden assumptions about a probability model do not creep in. The RFC says queueing drops are usually deterministic, and that this does not stop stochastic models being used to understand performance.

A metric whose value depends on the packet is named for a packet of type P, as in IP-type-P-connectivity. Metrics are defined for IP addresses (Src and Dst) rather than hosts, because a host can attach to more than one network.

Unless stated otherwise a packet is assumed to be standard formed: its IP length matches its contents, the version is 4, the header length is at least 5, the checksum is correct, it is not a fragment, it has enough TTL to arrive or the maximum TTL of 255, and it carries no IP options. A minimal IP packet is a standard-formed packet with a 0-octet payload and no options.

On security, the RFC says the topics it covers do not affect Internet security, but active measurement can be abused for denial-of-service attacks and passive recording can expose traffic, so each metric must have its own security discussion.
sections.eli5: When you measure, say exactly which kind of package you used and which door it went through, so someone else can repeat it and get the same answer.
